chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ahmad ibn al-Walid (may God be pleased with him) narrated that Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Khattab, from Ja'far ibn Bashir, from Abi Ayyanah, from al-Mansur ibn Hazim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

Three occasions on which supplication is returned to them in the plural although they are singular: when a man sneezes and it is said to him, 'May God have mercy upon you,' as if someone else is with him; and when a man greets another man and says, 'Peace be upon you,' and when a man prays for another man and says, 'May God grant you health.'

The compiler of this book - may God increase his honor - said: To the sneezer who is a disbeliever it is said, 'May God have mercy upon you two,' and the reference is to the two angels appointed over him, but as for the believer, it is said to him, 'May God have mercy upon you,' when he sneezes.

key_terms.يَرْحَمُكُمُ اللَّهُ: May God have mercy upon you (plural)

ai.seo_question: Why is the plural form of 'mercy' used when addressing a single person who sneezes in Islamic tradition?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Saduq highlights the linguistic nuance in Shia jurisprudence where the plural pronoun 'you' (kum) is applied to a single person to denote the presence of divine or angelic witnesses, specifically in the contexts of sneezing, greeting, and supplication. The compiler’s addition clarifies the theological distinction: for the believer, the plural signifies the mercy of the recording angels (Kiraman Katibin), whereas for the disbeliever, it refers strictly to the two angels tasked with recording their deeds, reflecting the concept of individual accountability accompanied by divine observation.
